question.text:
A portfolio manager is analyzing the performance of a mixed-asset portfolio consisting of 40% equities, 40% bonds, and 20% commodities. The expected return of equities is 10%, bonds is 5%, and commodities is 8%. The standard deviation of equities is 12%, bonds is 6%, and commodities is 10%. The risk-free rate is 3%. The correlations between the asset classes are as follows: equities and bonds: 0.2, equities and commodities: 0.4, bonds and commodities: 0.3.
What is the portfolio's Sharpe Ratio?

explanation.text: The Logic: Sharpe ratio = (portfolio expected return - risk-free rate) / portfolio standard deviation. Using the weighted-average portfolio return of 7.60%, the risk-free rate of 3.00%, and an approximate portfolio standard deviation of 6.93% from the covariance-weighted formula gives (7.60% - 3.00%) / 6.93% which is approximately 0.66. The Trap: 0.45, 0.85, and 1.10 tempt candidates who use the wrong numerator (raw return rather than excess return), apply an incorrect standard deviation, or invert the ratio. The defining feature of Sharpe is excess return per unit of total risk. Note: The Sharpe ratio definition as excess return divided by portfolio standard deviation is given in the source workbook on the cited page.
